claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles requires precisely synchronized reduction kinetics for all metal precursors.
Synchronized precursor reduction produces nearly simultaneous nucleation.
Nearly simultaneous nucleation promotes interdiffusion and locks in a homogeneous alloy phase.
Any asynchronicity in reduction events causes elemental segregation.
Any asynchronicity in reduction events causes phase separation.
Any asynchronicity in reduction events causes higher decomposition temperatures.
The proposed starting system contains Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, and Cu salts at identical concentrations in aqueous solution.
Changing pH or reducing-agent concentration can synchronize the reduction kinetics of the five precursors.
Synchronous reduction facilitates rapid interdiffusion of metal atoms.
Thorough atomic mixing resulting from simultaneous nucleation prevents elemental segregation and phase separation.
Offset reduction events produce uneven nucleation and insufficient atomic intermixing.
Uneven nucleation and insufficient atomic intermixing lead to phase heterogeneity.
Synchronizing reduction will produce a more homogeneous alloy phase than an asynchronous baseline.
Synchronizing reduction will lower decomposition temperatures relative to an asynchronous baseline.
Synchronizing reduction will increase the density of exposed catalytic surface atoms relative to an asynchronous baseline.
Asynchronous baseline synthesis produces phase separation and irregular nanoparticle morphologies.
The mechanism applies to aqueous systems in which noble-metal salt reduction kinetics can be finely controlled chemically.
The mechanism may not apply when intrinsic redox disparities cannot be reconciled or when nonaqueous or templated synthesis is used.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes tuning pH, while the falsification design states that pH remains constant. The design does not clearly identify what adjustment creates synchronization or the intentional timing mismatch if pH and the other listed conditions are fixed.

The comparison condition is described once as a baseline with unconstrained reduction timing and elsewhere as a control with an intentionally introduced timing mismatch; these are not necessarily the same control.
